question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Portuguese trading posts and their locations]
options: Hormuz – Entrance to the Persian Gulf
wrong_fact: Calicut (Kozhikode) is located on the Malabar Coast (western coast of India in Kerala), NOT on the eastern Coromandel Coast.
explanation: Calicut (Kozhikode) was the first port visited by Vasco da Gama in 1498 and is situated on the Malabar Coast (western coast of India). The Coromandel Coast is on the eastern side. Goa on the Konkan coast, Hormuz at the Persian Gulf entrance, and Malacca on the Malay Peninsula are all correctly matched.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Rivals who challenged Portuguese dominance and their primary base]
options: Dutch – Batavia (present-day Jakarta) as their Asian headquarters
English – Surat as their first major factory in India
French – Pondicherry as their main base in India
Ottomans – Lisbon as their naval base challenging Portugal
wrong_fact: The Ottomans challenged Portuguese naval dominance from their bases in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf (e.g., Aden, Basra), NOT from Lisbon, which was the Portuguese capital itself.
explanation: The Ottoman Empire challenged Portuguese trade routes from bases in the Middle East — particularly the Red Sea (Aden) and Persian Gulf region — supporting Muslim merchants against the Portuguese. Batavia was indeed the Dutch Asian HQ; Surat was the first English factory (1608/1613); and Pondicherry was the main French base in India.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Factor causing Portuguese decline and the geographic region most affected]
options: Loss of spice trade monopoly – Indian Ocean and Spice Islands (Maluku)
Union with Spain (1580) – Atlantic diversion of Portuguese naval resources
Dutch naval superiority – Bay of Bengal and Strait of Malacca
Ottoman control of overland spice routes – Cape of Good Hope route becoming irrelevant
wrong_fact: The Ottoman control of overland spice routes actually INCREASED the importance of the Cape of Good Hope route (which Portugal pioneered), not made it irrelevant. The Cape route gave Portugal an advantage over overland routes.
explanation: Portugal's Cape of Good Hope sea route around Africa was developed precisely to bypass Ottoman-controlled overland spice routes — this was a Portuguese advantage, not a cause of decline. Portuguese decline stemmed from Dutch/English naval challenge in the Indian Ocean, the Spanish Union diverting resources, and loss of monopoly on the spice trade.
